title: Unit Economics
subtitle: Profit per unit - the foundation of every business model
openingOptions: Customers stay loyal for 3 years on average before they leave the service for good elsewhere
Lifetime Value is 3 times the cost of acquiring a customer - the business model is viable
explanation: Unit economics asks a very specific question: does serving one more customer earn a profit or a loss? The two key figures are the cost of acquiring a customer and the profit that customer generates over their lifetime; a ratio of three or higher is usually considered the threshold for being able to scale profitably. The point most often missed is payback time: a model with a beautiful ratio that takes two years to recover its acquisition cost still burns cash while growing fast.

Calculate the profit that customer generates over their lifetime
Three or higher and scaling becomes profitable

realWorldExample.description: Many early-stage ride-hailing startups accepted an LTV/CAC below 1 for years - spending more on promotions to acquire customers than the value those customers brought in - betting that once they reached sufficient scale, acquisition cost would fall and LTV would rise thanks to network effects.

quiz.question: What is Contribution Margin?
options: Gross Profit, i.e. revenue minus the full cost of goods sold that period
After-tax profit allocated to each unit of product sold
Net revenue after discounts and returns are deducted
Revenue minus variable costs - the amount left to cover fixed costs
quiz.explanation: CM = Revenue − Variable Costs. CM/Revenue = CM%. A high CM% means each additional unit sold contributes more toward fixed costs and profit. SaaS businesses typically run CM% above 70%.

quiz.question: A startup has LTV/CAC = 0.8 (below 1) but is growing its customer count very fast. What is actually happening financially?
options: Losing money on each new customer - growing faster just burns cash faster
The business model is very good, because customer growth is fast
An LTV/CAC below 1 isn't a meaningful concern at an early stage
It will certainly succeed eventually because fast growth is always a good sign
quiz.explanation: An LTV/CAC below 1 is a serious warning: each new customer is actually making the company lose MORE money, not earn more. Fast growth in this situation is really just "burn-fueled growth".

quiz.question: LTV is 3 million, CAC is 1.5 million. What is the LTV/CAC ratio, and is it healthy?
options: 0.5x - below 1 means a loss on each new customer
2.0x - below the threshold of 3 usually considered healthy
4.5x - multiplying the two figures together
1.5x - taking the difference between LTV and CAC as the ratio
quiz.explanation: LTV/CAC = 3/1.5 = 2.0. The industry typically uses 3 as the healthy benchmark, so a level of 2 isn't disastrous but shows acquisition cost is eating too much into lifetime value.

quiz.question: Why is fast growth dangerous for a startup with LTV/CAC below 1?
options: Because investors will demand a lower valuation in the next round
Because fast growth always pulls operating costs up along with it
Because every new customer makes the loss even bigger
Because new customers tend to churn sooner than existing ones
quiz.explanation: Spending more than you earn on each customer means growth is multiplying the loss. Revenue looks pretty on the slide while cash runs out faster - this is how many startups die while looking like they're succeeding.

quiz.question: What does CAC Payback Period measure?
options: How long it takes for customer acquisition cost to start falling on its own
How long until a customer stops using the product and leaves
How long it takes the business to recoup its entire investment
How long it takes to recover the cost spent on acquiring a customer
quiz.explanation: This metric matters because cash goes out first and comes back later. A 6-month payback allows fast reinvestment; a 24-month payback means having two years of cash on hand ready for every growth cycle.

keyTakeaways: CAC Payback Period: time to recover customer acquisition cost

practicePrompt.question: A startup has LTV (customer lifetime value) = 3 million dong, CAC (cost to acquire one customer) = 2 million dong. The LTV/CAC ratio is 1.5. How should an investor assess this business model?
options: Worrying: an LTV/CAC of 1.5 sits well below the commonly used safety threshold of 3
Very good, since LTV/CAC > 1 means the company is already profitable on every customer it acquires
No need to worry about this ratio at all, since a startup's business model always needs time to be optimized
LTV/CAC has no meaning at all for companies in the early growth stage
practicePrompt.explanation: LTV/CAC ≥ 3: a viable business model - this is the common threshold venture investors use to assess a company. LTV/CAC = 1.5 means the company has almost no real margin left after acquisition cost and other operating costs are deducted - the business model isn't yet sustainable.

summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to a real decision.
summary.action: CAC Payback Period: time to recover customer acquisition cost

application.title: Calculate your own CAC/LTV
application.message: If you've ever sold something, freelanced, or run a small business, try estimating a customer's LTV and the CAC you spent to acquire that customer - see whether your LTV/CAC ratio reaches the 3x threshold.
application.secondary: You don't need exact figures - even a rough estimate gives you a useful perspective.

sections.text: Unit Economics is the most basic question every business model, whether a startup or a corporation, must answer: is each individual customer actually profitable? If the answer is no, growing fast just means burning cash faster.
LTV, CAC and the golden 3:1 ratio

LTV (Lifetime Value) is the total revenue or profit a customer generates over their entire time using the product. CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost) is the cost spent to acquire a new customer (marketing, sales, promotions). An LTV/CAC ratio ≥ 3 is seen as the benchmark for a sustainable business model - meaning the value returned is at least 3 times the cost spent to acquire that customer.
When LTV/CAC is below 1: growth is burning cash

A startup with LTV/CAC = 0.8 (below 1) but growing its customer count very fast is actually losing money on each new customer - the faster it grows, the faster it burns cash, because each new customer brings in less value than it costs to acquire them. Many early-stage ride-hailing startups accepted this situation for years, spending more on promotions than the value customers brought in, betting that at sufficient scale, CAC would fall and LTV would rise thanks to network effects. This strategy is only sustainable if the company has a clear plan to improve this ratio before it runs out of capital.

items: Contribution Margin = Revenue − Variable Costs - the portion that covers fixed costs and generates profit (SaaS businesses typically have CM% above 70%)
CAC Payback Period: the time needed to recover the cost of acquiring one customer
LTV/CAC ≥ 3: viable model; ~1: breakeven; below 1: losing money on each new customer

lines: Fast growth is only worth celebrating when unit economics hold up - otherwise, it's just a faster rate of burning cash.
